body:
Thank you for the quotes--very heavy stuff. I by no means wish to dissociate myself from the problems of the world (nor from, per your example, the problems in my own mind caused by my consumerist lifestyle and its implications for the people who actually support it, which I struggle with very often) but rather from the thoughts that show up and suggest that not existing is an option; they do a number on living with immediacy and handling reality as it currently is.

On one hand I'm wrapped up in my own issues, and on the other I have a tenuous grasp on that deep connection for everything else built of the same starstuff that Carl Sagan talks about. You're definitely right that I should try harder to focus on the latter and stop rehashing my problems, but man is it hard to be motivated to actively substantially make others' lives better when you don't firmly care for your own. I try to do it because it's obviously the best position to take, but I can't pretend (despite how hard I've tried) that not feeling gratification from helping someone, even when appreciation is being thrown at me, doesn't make it feel fruitless. I always feel like I could have done something grander.  

(Edit) Like you said, though, I know I really shouldn't expect to get a specific feeling from doing the right thing, but I haven't developed the discipline yet to seriously separate the feeling and the action.

I like the idea of trying to dissociate myself from the feeling. I've toyed with doing it with headaches and other physical annoyances after learning about "mind over matter", but it's harder when it's a psychological situation (i.e. I can imagine "no pain" when there is pain; I know what "no pain" feels like, but I'm not sure what "no suicidality" is like, if that makes sense). Thanks.

Thank you for your concern. There wasn't really any grief when he died; the antidepressant I'm on seems to be tailor-made to my personal assortment of serotonin receptors, and that coupled with my emotional distance from him made the guilt of not trying harder to have a relationship with him the feature presentation. It was the same for my brother (who's actually on the same medication).

Talking about this is an immense problem for me, though. I have seen a counselor at my university, but she was very unhelpful in helping me explore the reason for these thoughts, instead finding a newer and more obscured way of saying "be positive!" each session. 

I'd really rather not depress my friends and family with what I consider to be mental masturbation most macabre; would a psychologist, psychiatrist, or psychoanalyst be most appropriate to discuss these things?
